title: Secria
hook: A self-hosted secrets manager with envelope encryption and a CLI-native workflow.
text: Secria keeps application secrets out of .env files and chat messages. Values are envelope-encrypted, scoped to a project and environment, and revealed only through an audited path — from the web app or the CLI.
highlights: Envelope encryption: a master key wraps per-project keys, which encrypt each secret version.
Project- and environment-scoped access, with audited reveals that never log values.
A CLI workflow - run, diff, push, pull - injects secrets in memory.
Self-hosted on Cloud Run, with the client on Vercel and keys kept outside both.
coverAlt: Secria's landing page: a pale lock plate between two lime waveforms on a deep teal background.
galleryAlt: Secria's security section showing the master-key, project-key and secret-value chain beside a ciphertext sample.

caseStudy.problem: Secrets end up in .env files, screenshots and chat threads. I wanted a small, self-hosted vault that a solo developer could actually run, with a clear key hierarchy and an audit trail that records actions rather than values.
caseStudy.approach: I built Secria around envelope encryption: one master key, a per-project data key, and AES-256-GCM for every secret version. The web app never decrypts; access is scoped by workspace, project and environment, and every reveal or download is logged. A Python CLI handles push, pull, diff and run with secrets injected in memory.
caseStudy.outcome: Secria runs as a self-hosted service with a public landing page and CLI docs. It is already used to sync deployment secrets for some of my Cloud Run projects.
caseStudy.learned: Security is mostly about refusing convenience. The interface is small because every extra place plaintext can appear is another place it can leak.
